title: Chapter 87 — The Grand Armada
paragraphs: The long and narrow peninsula of Malacca, extending southeast from the territories of Burma, forms the most southerly point of all Asia. In a continuous line from that peninsula stretch the long islands of Sumatra, Java, Bali, and Timor. These, with many others, form a vast wall, lengthwise connecting Asia with Australia and dividing the long unbroken Indian Ocean from the densely studded eastern archipelagoes. This rampart is pierced by several passages for the convenience of ships and whales, the most prominent being the Straits of Sunda and Malacca. By the Straits of Sunda, chiefly, vessels bound to China from the west emerge into the China seas.

Those narrow Straits of Sunda divide Sumatra from Java. Standing midway in that vast rampart of islands, buttressed by that bold green promontory known to seamen as Java Head, they closely resemble the central gateway opening into some vast walled empire. And considering the inexhaustible wealth of spices, silks, jewels, gold, and ivory with which the thousand islands of that eastern sea are enriched, it seems a significant provision of nature that such treasures, by the very formation of the land, should at least bear the appearance — however ineffective — of being guarded from the all-grasping western world. The shores of the Straits of Sunda are unsupplied with those domineering fortresses which guard the entrances to the Mediterranean, the Baltic, and the Propontis. Unlike the Danes, these Orientals do not demand the obsequious homage of lowered topsails from the endless procession of ships that for centuries past, by night and day, have passed between Sumatra and Java, freighted with the costliest cargoes of the east. But while they freely waive such ceremony, they by no means renounce their claim to more solid tribute.

Since time out of mind, the pirate boats of the Malays, lurking among the low, shaded coves and islets of Sumatra, have sailed out upon passing vessels, fiercely demanding tribute at spear-point. Though by repeated bloody punishments at the hands of European warships their boldness has of late been somewhat checked, even now we occasionally hear of English and American vessels that have been ruthlessly boarded and plundered in those waters.

With a fair, fresh wind, the Pequod was now drawing near to these straits. Ahab intended to pass through them into the Java Sea, and thence, cruising northward over waters known to be frequented by the sperm whale, sweep inshore by the Philippine Islands and reach the far coast of Japan in time for the great whaling season there. By this route, the circumnavigating Pequod would sweep almost all the known sperm whale cruising grounds of the world before descending upon the equator in the Pacific — where Ahab, though everywhere else frustrated in his pursuit, firmly counted on giving battle to Moby Dick in the sea he was most known to frequent, at a season when he might most reasonably be expected to haunt it.

But how now? In this far-ranging quest, does Ahab touch no land? Does his crew drink air? Surely he will stop for water. No. For a long time now, the circus-running sun has raced within his fiery ring and needs no sustenance but what is in himself. So with Ahab. Mark this, too, about the whaler. While other ships are loaded down with foreign goods to be transferred to distant wharves, the world-wandering whale-ship carries no cargo but herself and her crew, their weapons and their wants. She has a whole lake's contents bottled in her ample hold. She is ballasted with useful things, not entirely with useless pig-lead and ballast iron. She carries years' worth of water in her. Clear old prime Nantucket water, which, when three years at sea, the Nantucketer in the Pacific prefers to drink over the brackish fluid rafted off only yesterday in casks from Peruvian or Indian streams. Hence it is that while other ships may have gone to China from New York and back again, touching at a score of ports, the whale-ship in all that time may not have sighted one grain of soil — her crew having seen no man but floating seamen like themselves. So that did you carry them the news that another flood had come, they would only answer: "Well, boys, here's the ark!"

Now, as many sperm whales had been captured off the western coast of Java, near the Straits of Sunda, and since most of the surrounding waters were generally recognized by fishermen as an excellent cruising ground, the Pequod's lookouts were repeatedly hailed and warned to stay wide awake as she gained upon Java Head. But though the green palmy cliffs of the land soon loomed on the starboard bow, and with delighted nostrils the fresh cinnamon was sniffed in the air, yet not a single spout was sighted. Almost giving up all thought of finding any whales in these parts, the ship had nearly entered the straits when the customary cheering cry was heard from aloft, and before long a spectacle of singular magnificence greeted us.

But here it must be noted that owing to the relentless activity with which sperm whales have lately been hunted over all four oceans, they now frequently gather in extensive herds, instead of almost invariably sailing in small, separate groups as in former times. Sometimes these herds embrace so great a multitude that it would almost seem as if numerous nations of them had sworn a solemn pact for mutual assistance and protection. To this massing of sperm whales may be attributed the fact that even in the best cruising grounds, you may now sometimes sail for weeks and months without being greeted by a single spout — and then be suddenly confronted by what seems thousands upon thousands.

Broad on both bows, at a distance of two or three miles, forming a great semicircle that embraced one half of the level horizon, a continuous chain of whale-spouts was playing and sparkling in the noonday air. Unlike the straight perpendicular twin-jets of the right whale, which divide at the top and fall over in two branches like the drooping boughs of a willow, the single forward-slanting spout of the sperm whale presents a thick curled bush of white mist, continually rising and falling away to leeward.

Seen from the Pequod's deck as she would rise on a high hill of the sea, this host of vapory spouts, individually curling up into the air and viewed through a blending atmosphere of bluish haze, looked like the thousand cheerful chimneys of some dense city, glimpsed on a balmy autumn morning by some horseman on a hill.

As marching armies approaching an unfriendly mountain pass accelerate their march, all eagerness to put that perilous passage behind them and once more expand in comparative safety upon the plain — even so did this vast fleet of whales now seem hurrying forward through the straits, gradually contracting the wings of their semicircle and swimming on in one solid but still crescent-shaped formation.

Crowding on all sail, the Pequod pressed after them. The harpooners handled their weapons and cheered loudly from the bows of their still-suspended boats. If the wind only held, they had little doubt that chased through these Straits of Sunda, the vast host would only spread out into the eastern seas to witness the capture of not a few of their number. And who could tell whether, in that gathered caravan, Moby Dick himself might not be temporarily swimming, like the worshipped white elephant in a Siamese coronation procession! So with every sail set, we drove these leviathans before us — when suddenly, the voice of Tashtego was heard, loudly directing attention to something in our wake.

Corresponding to the crescent ahead of us, we saw another behind us. It seemed formed of detached white vapors, rising and falling somewhat like whale-spouts, only they did not fully come and go but constantly hovered without quite disappearing. Leveling his glass at this sight, Ahab quickly spun in his pivot-hole, crying: "Aloft there, and rig whips and buckets to wet the sails! Malays, sir, and after us!"

As if lurking too long behind the headlands, waiting until the Pequod had fairly entered the straits, these rascally Asians were now in hot pursuit to make up for their overcautious delay. But when the swift Pequod, with a fresh leading wind, was herself in hot chase — how very kind of these tawny philanthropists to help speed her on to her own chosen pursuit, serving as mere riding-crops and spurs to her. As Ahab paced the deck with glass under arm, in his forward turn beholding the monsters he chased and in his backward turn the bloodthirsty pirates chasing him — some such thought seemed his. And when he glanced upon the green walls of the watery passage through which the ship was sailing, and considered that through that gate lay the route to his vengeance, and saw how through that same gate he was now both chasing and being chased to his deadly end — and not only that, but a herd of remorseless wild pirates and inhuman atheistical devils were infernally cheering him on with their curses — when all these thoughts had passed through his brain, Ahab's brow was left gaunt and furrowed, like a black sand beach after some stormy tide has been gnawing it without being able to drag the firm thing from its place.

But thoughts like these troubled very few of the reckless crew. When, after steadily dropping the pirates astern, the Pequod at last shot past the vivid green Cockatoo Point on the Sumatra side, emerging upon the broad waters beyond, the harpooners seemed more grieved that the swift whales had been gaining on the ship than glad that the ship had so victoriously gained upon the Malays. But still driving on in the whales' wake, at length they seemed to slow their speed. Gradually the ship neared them. The wind dying away, word was passed to launch the boats. But no sooner did the herd — by some wonderful instinct of the sperm whale — become aware of the three boats coming after them, though still a mile behind, than they rallied again. Forming in close ranks and battalions, so that their spouts all looked like flashing lines of stacked bayonets, they moved on with redoubled speed.

Stripped to our shirts and drawers, we sprang to the oars. After several hours' pulling, we were almost ready to give up the chase when a general pausing commotion among the whales gave encouraging signs that they were now under the influence of that strange paralysis of indecision which, when fishermen see it in a whale, they say he is gallied. The compact martial columns in which they had been rapidly and steadily swimming now broke apart in one measureless rout. Like King Porus's elephants in the battle against Alexander, they seemed going mad with panic. Expanding in vast irregular circles in all directions, swimming aimlessly this way and that, they plainly showed their distracted terror by their short, thick spoutings. This was still more strangely shown by those among them who, completely paralyzed as it were, helplessly floated like waterlogged dismasted ships on the sea. Had these leviathans been but a flock of simple sheep pursued over a pasture by three fierce wolves, they could not possibly have shown such excessive dismay. But this occasional timidity is characteristic of almost all herding creatures. Though banding together in tens of thousands, the lion-maned buffaloes of the West have fled before a solitary horseman. Witness, too, all human beings — how when herded together in the sheepfold of a theater pit, they will at the slightest alarm of fire rush helter-skelter for the exits, crowding, trampling, jamming, and mercilessly crushing each other to death. Best, therefore, withhold any amazement at the strangely gallied whales before us, for there is no folly of the beasts of the earth which is not infinitely outdone by the madness of men.

Though many of the whales, as has been said, were in violent motion, as a whole the herd neither advanced nor retreated but collectively remained in one place. As is customary in such cases, the boats separated at once, each making for some lone whale on the outskirts of the shoal. In about three minutes, Queequeg's harpoon was flung. The stricken whale darted blinding spray in our faces, then ran away with us like light, steering straight for the heart of the herd. Though such a move by a harpooned whale is by no means unprecedented and indeed is almost always expected to some degree, it presents one of the more dangerous episodes of the fishery. For as the swift monster drags you deeper and deeper into the frantic shoal, you bid farewell to cautious living and exist only in a delirious rush.

As, blind and deaf, the whale plunged forward, as if by sheer speed to rid himself of the iron leech fastened to him — as we tore a white gash in the sea, menaced on all sides by the crazed creatures rushing to and fro around us — our beset boat was like a ship mobbed by icebergs in a tempest, striving to steer through their complicated channels and straits, not knowing at what moment it might be locked in and crushed.

But not a bit daunted, Queequeg steered us expertly — now sheering off from this monster directly across our route, now edging away from that one whose colossal flukes were suspended overhead — while all the time Starbuck stood in the bow, lance in hand, pricking aside whatever whales he could reach with short thrusts, for there was no time for long ones. Nor were the oarsmen quite idle, though their usual duty was now entirely suspended. They chiefly attended to the shouting part of the business. "Out of the way, Commodore!" cried one to a great whale that suddenly rose bodily to the surface and for an instant threatened to swamp us. "Hard down with your tail, there!" cried a second to another that, close to our gunwale, seemed calmly cooling himself with his own fan-like extremity.

All whaleboats carry certain curious devices, originally invented by the Nantucket Indians, called drags. Two thick squares of wood of equal size are stoutly clenched together so that they cross each other's grain at right angles. A line of considerable length is attached to the middle of this block, and the other end, being looped, can in a moment be fastened to a harpoon. It is chiefly among gallied whales that this drag is used. For then, more whales are close around you than you can possibly chase at one time. But sperm whales are not encountered every day, so when you can, you must kill all you can. And if you cannot kill them all at once, you must wound them so that they can be killed afterward at your leisure. Hence the drag comes into play. Our boat was furnished with three of them. The first and second were successfully thrown, and we saw the whales staggering off, fettered by the enormous sideways resistance of the towing drag. They were hampered like prisoners with chain and ball. But upon flinging the third, the clumsy wooden block caught under one of the boat's seats and in an instant tore it out and carried it away, dumping the oarsman into the boat's bottom as the seat slid from under him. On both sides the sea poured in at the damaged planks, but we stuffed two or three shirts in and so stopped the leaks for the time being.

It would have been nearly impossible to throw these drag-harpoons had our whale's pace not greatly slowed as we advanced into the herd. Moreover, as we went still further from the circumference of commotion, the chaos seemed to be waning. So when at last the jerking harpoon pulled free and the towing whale vanished sideways, we glided with the tapering force of his parting momentum between two whales into the innermost heart of the shoal — as if from some mountain torrent we had slid into a serene valley lake. Here the storms raging in the gaps between the outermost whales were heard but not felt. In this central expanse, the sea presented that smooth satin-like surface called a sleek, produced by the subtle moisture thrown off by the whale in his quieter moods. Yes, we were now in that enchanted calm which they say lurks at the heart of every commotion. And still in the distracted distance we saw the tumults of the outer concentric circles — successive pods of whales, eight or ten in each, swiftly going round and round like multiplied teams of horses in a ring, so closely shoulder to shoulder that a titanic circus-rider might easily have arched over the middle ones and ridden round on their backs. Owing to the density of the whales reposing more immediately around the trapped center of the herd, no possible chance of escape was presently offered to us. We had to watch for a breach in the living wall that hemmed us in — the wall that had only admitted us in order to shut us up. Keeping to the center of the lake, we were occasionally visited by small, tame cows and calves: the women and children of this routed host.

Now, including the occasional wide intervals between the revolving outer circles and the spaces between the various pods in any one of those circles, the entire area at this point must have contained at least two or three square miles. At any rate — though such a measurement at such a time might be deceptive — spouts could be seen from our low boat that seemed to play up almost from the rim of the horizon. I mention this because, as if the cows and calves had been purposely locked up in this innermost fold, and as if the wide extent of the herd had prevented them from learning the precise cause of its stopping — or possibly, being so young, innocent, and inexperienced — however it may have been, these smaller whales, now and then visiting our becalmed boat from the margin of the lake, showed a wondrous fearlessness and confidence, or else a spellbound panic that was impossible not to marvel at. Like household dogs, they came snuffling right up to our gunwales and touching them, until it almost seemed that some enchantment had suddenly domesticated them. Queequeg patted their foreheads. Starbuck scratched their backs with his lance, though, fearful of the consequences, he refrained from darting it for the time.

But far beneath this wondrous world upon the surface, another and still stranger world met our eyes as we gazed over the side. For suspended in those watery vaults floated the forms of nursing mother whales, and those that by their enormous girth seemed shortly to become mothers. The lake, as I have hinted, was to a considerable depth exceedingly transparent. And as human infants while suckling will calmly and fixedly gaze away from the breast, as if leading two different lives at the same time — while yet drawing mortal nourishment, still spiritually feasting upon some unearthly memory — even so did the young of these whales seem to look up toward us, but not at us, as if we were but a bit of seaweed in their newborn sight. Floating on their sides, the mothers also seemed quietly eyeing us. One of these little infants, that from certain signs seemed hardly a day old, might have measured some fourteen feet in length and six feet around. He was a little frisky, though his body seemed scarcely recovered from the cramped position it had so recently occupied in the womb, where, tail to head and all ready for the final spring, the unborn whale lies bent like a Tartar's bow. The delicate side-fins and the palms of his flukes still freshly retained the plaited, crumpled appearance of a baby's ears newly arrived from foreign parts.
"Line! Line!" cried Queequeg, looking over the gunwale. "Him fast! Him fast! Who line him? Who struck? Two whale — one big, one little!"
"What ails you, man?" cried Starbuck.
"Look here," said Queequeg, pointing down.

As when the struck whale that from the tub has reeled out hundreds of fathoms of rope — as, after deep sounding, he floats up again and shows the slackened curling line buoyantly rising and spiraling toward the air — so now Starbuck saw long coils of the umbilical cord of Madame Leviathan, by which the young cub seemed still tethered to its mother. Not seldom in the rapid turns of the chase, this natural line, with the maternal end loose, becomes entangled with the hemp one, so that the cub is trapped. Some of the subtlest secrets of the seas seemed revealed to us in this enchanted pond. We saw young Leviathan courtship in the deep.*

*The sperm whale, like all other species of Leviathan but unlike most other fish, breeds indiscriminately at all seasons. After a gestation that may probably be set at nine months, it produces but one at a time, though in some few known instances giving birth to twins — a contingency provided for in suckling by two teats, curiously situated one on each side of the anus, though the breasts themselves extend upward from that point. When by chance these parts in a nursing whale are cut by the hunter's lance, the mother's pouring milk and blood discolor the sea in rivaling streams for yards. The milk is very sweet and rich. It has been tasted by man, and it might go well with strawberries. When overflowing with mutual affection, the whales greet each other in human fashion.

And thus, though surrounded by circle upon circle of terrors and frights, did these inscrutable creatures at the center freely and fearlessly indulge in all peaceful pursuits — yea, serenely reveling in tenderness and delight. But even so, amid the tornadoed Atlantic of my being, do I myself still forever centrally float in mute calm. And while ponderous planets of unceasing woe revolve around me, deep down and deep inland there I still bathe myself in an eternal mildness of joy.

Meanwhile, as we lay entranced, the occasional sudden frantic scenes in the distance showed the activity of the other boats, still engaged in dragging the whales on the frontier of the host, or possibly carrying on the war within the first circle, where there was room enough and some convenient retreats. But the sight of the enraged dragged whales now and then blindly darting to and fro across the circles was nothing to what at last met our eyes. It is sometimes the custom, when fast to a whale more than usually powerful and alert, to try to hamstring him by severing or maiming his gigantic tail-tendon. This is done by throwing a short-handled cutting-spade with a rope attached for hauling it back. A whale wounded in this way — as we afterward learned — but not effectively, had broken away from the boat, carrying along with him half of the harpoon line. In the extraordinary agony of the wound, he was now dashing among the revolving circles like the lone mounted desperado Arnold at the Battle of Saratoga, carrying dismay wherever he went.

But agonizing as this whale's wound was, and appalling a spectacle in itself, the peculiar horror he seemed to inspire in the rest of the herd was owing to a cause which at first the intervening distance hid from us. But at length we saw that by one of the unimaginable accidents of the fishery, this whale had become entangled in the harpoon line he towed. He had also run off with the cutting-spade in him. While the free end of the rope attached to that weapon had permanently caught in the coils of the harpoon line wound around his tail, the cutting-spade itself had worked loose from his flesh. So, tormented to madness, he was now churning through the water, violently flailing with his flexible tail and tossing the keen spade about him, wounding and killing his own companions.

This terrific sight seemed to rouse the whole herd from their frozen fright. First, the whales forming the margin of our lake began to crowd a little and jostle against each other, as if lifted by spent waves from afar. Then the lake itself began faintly to heave and swell. The submarine nurseries and bridal chambers vanished. In tighter and tighter orbits, the whales in the more central circles began to swim in thickening clusters. Yes, the long calm was departing. A low advancing hum was soon heard. And then, like the tumultuous masses of block-ice when the great river Hudson breaks up in spring, the entire host of whales came tumbling upon their inner center, as if to pile themselves up in one common mountain. Instantly Starbuck and Queequeg changed places, Starbuck taking the stern.

"Oars! Oars!" he intensely whispered, seizing the helm. "Grip your oars and clench your souls now! My God, men, stand by! Shove him off, Queequeg — the whale there! Prick him! Hit him! Stand up — stand up, and stay so! Spring, men — pull, men! Never mind their backs — scrape them! Scrape away!"

The boat was now all but jammed between two vast black hulks, leaving a narrow strait between their long bodies. But by desperate effort we at last shot into a temporary opening, then pulled hard, earnestly watching for another way out. After many similar narrow escapes, we at last swiftly glided into what had just been one of the outer circles but was now crossed by random whales, all violently making for the center. This lucky escape was cheaply purchased by the loss of Queequeg's hat, which, while he stood in the bow pricking the fleeing whales, was snatched clean from his head by the air-current made by the sudden tossing of a pair of broad flukes close by.

Riotous and disordered as the universal commotion now was, it soon resolved itself into what seemed a systematic movement. Having clumped together at last in one dense body, the whales renewed their forward flight with increased speed. Further pursuit was useless, but the boats still lingered in their wake to pick up whatever dragged whales might be dropped behind, and also to secure one that Flask had killed and marked. The mark is a pennanted pole, two or three of which are carried by every boat. When additional prey is at hand, these are inserted upright into the floating body of a dead whale, both to mark its place on the sea and as a token of prior possession, should the boats of any other ship draw near.

The result of this hunt was somewhat illustrative of that wise saying in the fishery: the more whales, the less fish. Of all the dragged whales, only one was captured. The rest managed to escape for the time, but only to be taken, as will later be seen, by some other vessel than the Pequod.
